newsitem.title: INDIA: Israel gets flak, Arafat sympathy from Non-Aligned.
newsitem.headline: Israel gets flak, Arafat sympathy from Non-Aligned.

text.p: More than 100 developing nations opened a two-day meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement (MAM) on Monday with calls for the expansion of the United Nation Security Council and denunciations of Israel.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan joined Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda in calling for greater representation of poor countries on the powerful U.N. body -- one of the themes of the NAM ministerial conference.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, a surprise guest, accused Israel of harming the Middle East peace process.
Arafat said Israel had used U.S. vetoes in the U.N. Security Council to prevent action against Israel's plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews on land captured in the 1967 Middle East war.
Ties between Palestinians and Israelis plunged into crisis after the Israeli government broke ground on the settlement. "It is a declaration of war against the peace process," Arafat said.
Arafat's appearance at the New Delhi meeting was welcomed by Iranian delegates headed by Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati.
The Non-Aligned Movement, formed in 1961 at the height of the Cold War, has 113 members, most of them developing nations.
Arafat appealed to delegates to help convene an early special meeting of the U.N. General Assembly to discuss the Middle East. He said recent Security Council meetings had failed to yield any result.
Arafat urged NAM members to follow recent resolutions of the Arab League seeking to review diplomatic ties with Israel.
The NAM meeting adopted Arafat's speech as part of the official proceedings of the New Delhi meeting, which is working towards an overall political declaration on Tuesday.
Colombian Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia said that as chair of the meeting, she had sent a letter to Annan requesting a special session of the General Assembly on the Middle East.

"It is with deep concern that we have been observing the increasing deterioration in the peace process in the Middle East," Mejia said. "We cannot but demand the immediate cessation of construction of Israeli settlements in Jabal Abdul Ghneim in East Jerusalem."
Middle East peace talks were halted after Israel began work last month on the new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, sparking daily clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops.
U.N. reform and the Middle East were among a handful of issues sure to dominate the New Delhi meeting, which was given unusual prominence by the presence of the U.N. chief and Arafat.

An Indian Foreign Ministry spokesman said a NAM committee on Palestine was to discuss the Middle East peace process later on Monday, and foreign ministers in a brainstorming session were free to raise the issue but it was not on the official agenda.
The brainstorming session, which began after lunch, was to discuss the interest of developing countries in seeking the elimination of all nuclear weapons, the spokesman said.
Other items on the agenda included the relevance of NAM after the end of the Cold War and environmental issues concerning developing countries, he said.
Annan backed efforts to expand the U.N. Security Council, whose permanent members are the five declared nuclear powers -- Britain, China, France , Russia and the United States.
"The United Nations still reflects, in some ways -- for example, in the Security Council -- the geopolitical realities of the 1940s," he said.
New Delhi wants a permanent seat on the Security Council.

India's prime minister said the U.N. must be reformed to meet NAM's aspirations, and called for a redoubling of efforts to wipe out nuclear weapons. "The process of nuclear disarmament has to be accelerated," said Deve Gowda.
